---
title: "Quiz: fast MRI with compressed sensing"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** What does an MRI scanner measure, and why does the scan time depend on the number of k-space lines?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One readout = one line.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It measures Fourier coefficients of the object (k-space), one line per excitation. Each line costs a fixed repetition time, so the scan time is proportional to the number of lines: 256 × 128 lines at 10 ms take 5.5 minutes.
:::

---

**Q2.** You keep only the central quarter of the k-space lines. What does the zero-filled image look like? Can a sparsity prior repair it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which frequencies are missing?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A low-pass filtered image: blurred, with ringing near edges. A sparsity prior cannot bring back sharp edges reliably: the high frequencies were never measured, and the artefact (blur) is not noise-like but structured.
:::

---

**Q3.** You keep every second line. Where does the ghost appear?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Regular undersampling by r gives r copies.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A copy of the image shifted by half the field of view along the phase-encoding direction, overlapping the original (fold-over, aliasing).
:::

---

**Q4.** Why are the random lines drawn more densely near the centre of k-space?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where is the energy, and which wavelets live at low frequencies?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Most of the image energy is at low frequencies (77 % of the phantom's energy within the central 17 of 256 lines), and coarse wavelets are concentrated there: the low frequencies are coherent with the coarse wavelets, so they must be sampled (almost) completely. Fine wavelets are spread out over high frequencies, where sparse random sampling suffices.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why is the ISTA/FISTA step size τ = 1 safe for MRI with a Cartesian mask?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the norm of PF?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The forward operator keeps some rows of an orthonormal DFT: it has orthonormal rows, so its largest gain is 1 (L = 1) and τ ≤ 1/L = 1.
:::

---

**Q6.** A compressed-sensing reconstruction at 4× has a good PSNR. A radiologist asks whether a small, faint lesion could have been removed. What do you answer?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does ℓ1 do to small coefficients?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Yes, it could: ℓ1 sets small wavelet coefficients to zero and shrinks the rest, and a small low-contrast lesion consists only of small coefficients. The PSNR is dominated by the large structures and does not show it. In the phantom with five faint discs, they are gone already at 4×. Validate with phantoms or fully sampled reference scans for the kind of lesion that matters.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Show that keeping every second line ($k_y$ even) of an image of $N$ rows gives the average of the image and its copy shifted by $N/2$ rows.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write the even mask as ½(1 + e^{iπk_y}).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Along $y$ the mask is $\tfrac12(1 + e^{iπk_y})$. Multiplying the spectrum by $e^{iπk_y} = e^{2πik_y(N/2)/N}$ shifts the image by $N/2$ rows (shift theorem). So the zero-filled image is $\tfrac12(x(y) + x(y + N/2))$.
:::
